title: On the (im)possibility of fairness
abstract: What does it mean for an algorithm to be fair? Different papers use different notions of algorithmic fairness, and although these appear internally consistent, they also seem mutually incompatible. We present a mathematical setting in which the distinctions in previous papers can be made formal. In addition to characterizing the spaces of inputs (the "observed" space) and outputs (the "decision" space), we introduce the notion of a construct space: a space that captures unobservable, but meaningful variables for the prediction. We show that in order to prove desirable properties of the entire decision-making process, different mechanisms for fairness require different assumptions about the nature of the mapping from construct space to decision space. The results in this paper imply that future treatments of algorithmic fairness should more explicitly state assumptions about the relationship between constructs and observations.

claims.text: Under the What You See Is What You Get (WYSIWYG) worldview with error parameter delta, an individual fairness mechanism IFM_delta' guarantees (epsilon, epsilon')-fairness for a function f where epsilon' = f(delta, delta').

A discrete decision space disallows an individually fair mechanism and precludes (delta - epsilon, delta')-fairness under the WYSIWYG worldview with parameter epsilon for any delta, delta' < 1 and rich mechanism f.
Under the We're All Equal (WAE) worldview, a valid group fairness mechanism with parameter epsilon' guarantees (max(epsilon, epsilon')/delta)-nondiscrimination.
If structural bias exists in the mapping from construct space to observed space, applying an individual fairness mechanism results in discriminatory outcomes in the decision space.

Fairness mechanisms and non-discrimination mechanisms are tied to fundamentally conflicting worldviews (WYSIWYG versus Structural Bias/WAE) and cannot simultaneously guarantee fairness and non-discrimination without explicit axiomatic assumptions.

limitations.text: The construct space is inherently unobservable in real-world settings, making direct measurement of construct space features and distances impossible without adopting explicit worldview axioms.
Prior algorithmic fairness definitions rest on unstated assumptions about societal fairness that are mutually incompatible, rendering direct comparison of fair algorithms difficult.

future_work.text: Future treatments of algorithmic fairness should explicitly state assumptions about the relationship between construct space and observed space.

methodologies.name: Construct-Observed-Decision Space Mapping Framework
methodologies.description: A mathematical framework modeling decision pipelines as metric-space transformations using additive distortion, Wasserstein distance, and Gromov-Wasserstein distance to formalize individual fairness, group skew, and structural bias.
